articles.title_orig: Haiti strikes deal with El Salvador to build new prisons after minister visit
articles.title_zh: Haiti strikes deal with El Salvador to build new prisons after minister visit
articles.content_orig:
Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele said his forces struck the home of Jeff “Gwo Lwa” Larose, leader of the so-called ‘Taliban’ gang in Canaan on Nov. 18, calling the operation a gift to Haitians on the Battle of Vertières Day. The strike follows a similar operation against the residence of 400 Mawozo leader Wilson “Lanmò San Jou” Joseph and comes one day after Haiti signed a new security cooperation deal.
PORT-AU-PRINCE — Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele said Wednesday that his forces struck the home of Jeff “Gwo Lwa” Larose, leader of the so-called ‘Taliban’ gang in Canaan, an area north of Haiti’s capital.
Bukele called the operation a gift to Haitians on the anniversary of the Battle of Vertières , marking Salvadoran troops’ intensifying operations against criminal organizations in Haiti.
“[This is] my gift to the Haitian people on the anniversary of the Battle of Vertières,” Bukele said in a post on X.
A video accompanying the post showed helicopters and footage of the residence under attack. Bukele did not say whether the house had been destroyed or damaged. However, several local media outlets said the drone strikes destroyed the property.
Kado mwen pou pèp ayisyen an nan anivèsè Batay Vètyè a ❤️ pic.twitter.com/z3TO3UurAT
The operation marks the second reported strike on a gang leader’s residence by Salvadoran forces, following a Nov. 8 attack on the home of Wilson “Lanmò San Jou” Joseph, notorious leader of the 400 Mawozo gang.
Local media and residents in Canaan reported several explosions Wednesday morning, and helicopters were seen flying over areas near the capital.
Salvadoran forces, which deployed about 2,500 special troops to Haiti last month, have been conducting operations against gang strongholds. Their deployment is separate from the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force ( GSF ).
The operations also come amid efforts to locate four Salvadoran aviation technicians abducted Oct. 18 after a gang intercepted an ambulance in the Santo area of Croix-des-Bouquets. Still, their whereabouts and their fate remain unknown.
Salvadoran Minister of Justice and Public Security Gustavo Villatoro said Nov. 16 at the second International Conference on State and Democracy that Salvadoran troops would leave Haiti once the four technicians are found.
“If tomorrow they reappear, as President Bukele said, we will leave,” Villatoro said.
The operation in Canaan comes as Haiti seeks to strengthen its security partnership with El Salvador. During a Cabinet meeting Nov. 17, the Haitian government announced it had approved a bilateral cooperation agreement that Haiti signed with El Salvador.
“This decision marks a new step in strengthening bilateral relations and cooperation between the two countries, particularly in addressing the security challenges facing Haiti,” the government said in a statement .
Salvadoran forces have also participated in operations to regain control of key infrastructure, including the Sylvio Cator National Stadium and the headquarters of the state electricity company, Electricité d’Haïti (EDH), alongside the Haitian National Police (PNH), the prime minister’s office-led task force and the Haitian Armed Forces (FAd’H).
Also on Tuesday, thousands of Haitians took to the streets to express support and love for Bukele and Salvadoran troops. They urged them to continue their offensive against the gangs’ grip on the country.
Protesters called on Salvadoran forces to pursue and neutralize gang members, including through the use of drones.
People chanted in Haitian Creole, “ Ba yo dwonn ,” meaning “Strike them with drones” in English.
They warned that civilians would bear the brunt of the violence if foreign troops withdrew and gangs regained ground.
Bukele responded to images of the demonstrations in another post on X , expressing surprise at the show of support and confidence that Haitians would prevail against the gangs.
“I never expected something like this. I hear you loud and clear,” Bukele said. “I love you too. We will triumph. God will give us victory.”
I am Juhakenson Blaise, a journalist based in the city of Port-au-Prince, Haiti. I cover the news that develops in this city and deals with other subjects related to the experience of Haitians for the Haitian Times newspaper. I am also a lover of poetry.

articles.title_orig: Kalshi races to get ahead of New York order that could shut down exchange
articles.title_zh: Kalshi races to get ahead of New York order that could shut down exchange
articles.content_orig:
The battle between Kalshi and the state of New York is growing heated. An attorney for the the prediction market company warned they may have to stop all activity nationwide if a temporary restraining order goes into effect.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and state Attorney General Letitia James first announced a lawsuit against Kalshi in July for running what they called an “illegal gambling operation.” The state has sought a restraining order against Kalshi to keep the site from operating while the case is heard.
Kalshi’s attorneys argue that because the company is headquartered in New York, any enforcement action in that state will impact its ability to operate in other states . The Commodities Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), which under Donald Trump’s administration has gone to bat for Kalshi and other prediction markets like Polymarket, has argued that any shutdown of Kalshi in New York would be an “ existential threat ” to the business.
The CFTC has sued twelves states that have sought to restrict or completely ban Kalshi’s activities in their states, including New York. On Friday, a federal judge rejected CFTC’s attempt to block New York from any enforcement action, according to Reuters .Â U.S. District Judge Lorna Schofield in Manhattan wrote that the CFTC had “not established a likelihood of success on the merits” of its core argument, which is that the CFTC is Kalshi’s sector regulator, and that federal derivatives law preempts state gambling laws.
Utah has even brought criminal charges against Kalshi and its co-founders, Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara.
Kalshi wants New York’s case to be heard in federal court, but the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York ruled Thursday that the case could proceed in New York’s Supreme Court. (Reuters noted that the new ruling against the CFTC nonetheless increases the chances that the case will eventually be heard by the U.S. Supreme Court.)
Kalshi spokesperson Elisabeth Diana told Gizmodo in an email Friday that it has followed the law and has been regulated by the federal government since the Biden era.
âKalshi was certified as a federally regulated exchange under the Biden administration and has been compliant with the law since day one,” said Diana. “We want to work with the Governor and Attorney General on a resolution that protects the interests of the 1.2 million New Yorkers who use Kalshi.â
States have generally been allowed to make their own gambling laws, but the Trump administration has sought to protect Kalshi and Polymarket with their own lawsuits against state AGs. The president’s son, Donald Trump Jr., was hired as an advisor to both Kalshi and Polymarket when President Trump returned to office in 2025. Trump Jr. invested heavily in Polymarket, which led to a very public falling out with the company last week after Democrats stomped the GOP in this month’s midterm elections.
Kalshi argues that it’s not a gambling website because there’s no house and it doesn’t set odds. Users bet against each other, and the odds change based on how many people bet in one direction or another.
Prediction markets officially prohibit insider trading, but the definition of “insider trading” in any given context can be incredibly difficult to parse, given the wide variety of topics for wagers. That’s not even factoring in how difficult it can be to enforce. If your cousin’s wife randomly saw the playlist for the Super Bowl halftime show, and people are betting on the songs that will be played, is that insider knowledge? Even if it is, how can it be policed?
While the CFTC has generally defended the prediction markets under Trump, the regulator told Kalshi recently warned that it should shut down so-called “mention markets” about the president because they could be “readily susceptible to manipulation.” Mention markets allow people to bet on what words Trump will say. It was revealed over the summer that Trumpâs now-former teleprompter operator, Gabriel Perez , made about $100,000 on those markets.
A New York Supreme Court court hearing has been set for 11:30 a.m. ET on Monday in New York .

articles.title_orig: Top US Senate Democrat accuses Trump of putting national security at risk with AI chip sales to China
articles.title_zh: Top US Senate Democrat accuses Trump of putting national security at risk with AI chip sales to China
articles.content_orig:
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer on Friday accused President Donald Trump of putting US national security at risk by allowing advanced artificial intelligence chips to be exported to Chinese companies, including those with alleged ties to China's military.
Speaking on the Senate floor, Schumer cited information released by the House of Representatives showing that the Trump administration approved nearly 900,000 shipments of advanced AI chips to Chinese companies during the first six months after easing export restrictions.
The House Foreign Affairs Committee on Thursday disclosed that the Commerce Department approved 879,000 shipments of advanced Nvidia and AMD chips between December 2025 and May 2026.
The shipments included 75,000 chips for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent, 43,000 for Baidu, and 4,000 for BYD, all of which the Pentagon lists as companies allegedly linked to the Chinese military, according to the House committee.
Schumer alleged that the Commerce Department authorized the sale of tens of thousands of Nvidia chips to a company affiliated with a Chinese intelligence operative who had previously targeted former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
Last week, Huang resigned after 33 years as CEO, following reports of extramarital affairs, including an alleged relationship with a woman suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence.
Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick knew about the woman's alleged intelligence ties before the sales were approved, according to Schumer.
"Keep in mind, Trump and Lutnick knew this woman was a spy ahead of time, and still rushed to approve the sale of this sensitive technology to her companies," he said.
"Trump and Lutnick sold out America's national security to make a quick buck for themselves and their billionaire buddies," said Schumer, accusing the administration of prioritizing financial interests over US security and technological competitiveness.
The Democratic leader also criticized Trump's reception this week by Chinese officials, arguing that Beijing's warm welcome was connected to the administration's decision to loosen restrictions on advanced American semiconductor exports.
"Trump needs to realize that the only reason he received such a warm welcome from the Chinese Communist Party this week was because he's doling out our most advanced AI chips to China, like their party favors," he said.
Schumer urged Congress to pass three pieces of legislation to tighten oversight of AI chip exports: the AI Overwatch Act, the MATCH Act, and the Chips Security Act.
Schumer is seeking the post of Senate majority leader in the new Congress starting in January, in which Democrats are set to enjoy a 56-44 Senate majority over Republicans. One senator, Chris Van Hollen, is challenging Schumer for the job.
Democrats have pledged to carry out more vigorous oversight of the Trump administration once they take control of both the House of Representatives and Senate on Jan. 3.

articles.title_orig: NATO calls Russian missiles landing in Poland a 'grave violation' of airspace
articles.title_zh: NATO calls Russian missiles landing in Poland a 'grave violation' of airspace
articles.content_orig:
Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".
The moment of impact was caught by a camera on a farm, and officials later made clear there was no risk to residents.
Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.
He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," said Rutte, who was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday.
A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.
"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa Dęba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.
Hours later, five coalition defence ministers - from the UK, France, Poland, Estonia and Lithuania - visited the military training ground where the drill was taking place.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told reporters that what had happened earlier was "yet another example of Russian provocation that is designed to divide Europe and to deter Ukraine's allies from supporting their fight for freedom and democracy".
In Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the missile incident was "utterly unacceptable".
European Council President António Costa expressed his "strong solidarity" with the Polish people and said Russia had to come to the negotiating table to bring the war to the end.
The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.
At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.
Russia also launched an apparent double tap attack on the busy centre of the Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih.
The Chairman of the Kryvyi Rih Defense Council, Oleksandr Vilkul, said two people were killed in the shelling, including a 20-year-old woman and a seven-year-old boy, and at least 40 people have been injured.
This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland. In July a cruise missile also landed in Poland, leaving a 10m-wide (33ft) crater. That incident also took place during an attack on the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.
Casualties in Poland have been rare, while Ukraine suffers deadly attacks on a daily basis. However, two Polish farmers were killed by a missile in November 2022, which was believed to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile responding to a Russian attack.
Moldovan officials said on Friday that their airspace had also been violated on Friday, when a drone crossed briefly into its territory during Russia's attacks on Ukraine.
The Moldovan defence ministry has recorded 118 such violations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

articles.title_orig: Fresh off China Trip, Trump Bobs and Weaves in Freewheeling Press Conference
articles.title_zh: Fresh off China Trip, Trump Bobs and Weaves in Freewheeling Press Conference
articles.content_orig:
Trump, Xi and Putin don't have much to say after their historic meeting.
President Donald Trump is headed back to Washington after a historic trilateral meeting with presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia -- the first-ever sitdown between the three global superpowers -- with no tangible diplomatic breakthroughs in hand.
Following their meeting, the three leaders released what was described as a symbolic four-point "peace declaration," focusing on reform at the United Nations, oil supply, nuclear risk reduction and opposition to what it called the International Criminal Court's "jurisdiction abuse."
The symbolic peace declaration made no mention of Russia's war with Ukraine, which is in its fifth year, or the war with Iran. Both Russia and China have faced accusations by U.S. and European officials of providing satellite imagery and broader intelligence support to Iran, accusations both countries have denied.
Trump left Shenzhen without taking questions from reporters after the meeting but announced in a post on his social media platform while traveling back to Washington that he would hold a news conference at the White House on Friday.
Here are takeaways from Trump's trip:
The three leaders affirmed their commitment that nuclear war should never be fought but announced no commitments to reduce their respective nuclear arsenals.
Trump had insisted nuclear arms control be a central topic of the summit.
"As the world's three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia, and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth, and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used," Trump said in brief remarks ahead of the meeting. "The power is unbelievable, unthinkable."
"It's not an ​easy thing to do -- give them up," Trump said.
Trump also used the issue of nuclear proliferation to defend the U.S. war with Iran, repeating his assertion that Iran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon.
"It's also vital that we cooperate to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world. That's what we're doing in Iran. We're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon," he said.
In a joint statement released following the meeting, the three leaders said they had an "in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation" and "committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security."
Trump, Xi, and Putin said the three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.
The "peace declaration" released after the meeting made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the U.S.-led war in Iran.
"We are going to be discussing the war between Russia and Ukraine, and we already have. President Putin and I have had a long discussion today for quite a while. That's what pretty much what the discussion was about, and I think things are happening," Trump said.
For his part, Putin briefly commented on his escalating war in Ukraine during opening remarks.
"Our countries have numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine. We discussed this yesterday with the Chairman of the People's Republic of China and today at the initiative of the U.S. president, we devoted significant attention to this during our bilateral meeting," the Russian president said, speaking through a translator.
The leaders also declared they plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products "for the benefit of all nations" while also reaffirming the importance of the stable flow of energy.
The oil market has been roiled in the nine months of the U.S.'s war with Iran, with the critical waterway through which a fifth of the world's oil supplies has transited under constant threat. Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities have further exacerbated global energy flows.
There were no signs upon conclusion of their meeting that Trump secured any agreements from Xi or Putin to help solve the Iran conflict.
Trump also highlighted that the three would discuss the International Criminal Court, the international body that works to uphold international law and prosecute war crimes. The Trump administration has targeted the ICC and its judges with sanctions and has sharply criticized the body.
"In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nation's sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction," Trump said in his opening remarks.
As part of the peace declaration, the three heads of state "recognized that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction."
ABC News has reached out to the ICC for comment.

articles.title_orig: Michel Zecler: Police officers sentenced for beating of music producer
articles.title_zh: Michel Zecler: Police officers sentenced for beating of music producer
articles.content_orig:
Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.
The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.
Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.
Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.
Lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.
All were told they could never serve in the police again.
The case became a cause célèbre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.
Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.
This was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.
Because the racist element was accepted by the court, the sentences were toughened.
The case was heard by a panel of five judges.
The incident took place during the Covid lockdown in 2020. Zecler was accused by the officers for not wearing a mask when doing so was obligatory as he approached his studio on foot.
They later claimed his behaviour aroused their suspicions, and they thought he might be carrying drugs. No evidence of this emerged.
After Zecler entered the lobby, the police followed - without a warrant - and tried to bring him outside. Zecler refused to go out, and the beating ensued. Zecler cried for help and some people appeared from the basement and pushed the police outside.
The officers then smashed a glass pane and sent a tear-gas grenade into the building, forcing those inside to come out - after which Zecler was again hit. He was then arrested.
During the trial Zecler said had it not been for the CCTV video, he would have been in court not as a victim but as a potential criminal.
In their last words before the court, all three police officers apologised for what they had done. Tondeux said he was sorry "for the image of the police that I have given".

articles.title_orig: Treasury secretary says no further restrictions are needed for Nvidia chip exports to China
articles.title_zh: Treasury secretary says no further restrictions are needed for Nvidia chip exports to China
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday that no further restrictions on the sale of older Nvidia chips to China are needed following the Trump administration's move earlier this week to block China's remote access to the latest semiconductors.
The ability of Chinese tech firms to access Nvidia’s technology came under scrutiny after CEO Jensen Huang stepped down amid allegations of his affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that uses advanced chips to generate computing power that Chinese firms access remotely.
“The proper chip restrictions are in place,” Bessent said in an interview with CNBC after returning from a trip to Asia with President Donald Trump . “And the remote access has been curtailed.”
Bessent's comments came a day after the House Foreign Affairs Committee released details of the Commerce Department's approval of the sales of more than 850,000 chips from Nvidia and its competitor AMD to Chinese companies. The Pentagon has identified some of those companies as having ties to the Chinese military.
The report tracked applications from Nvidia to sell its H200 chips — one of its more powerful products, though not the most advanced — and AMD's applications to sell its roughly comparable MI325X chip to companies that are either located or headquartered in China, or entities with parent companies based in China.
The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security approved the export, re-export, or transfer of 879,868 of these chips to companies with Chinese ties across 21 license applications as of May 11, 2026, the report said. Nvidia and AMD had requested to sell a cumulative total of more than 3.4 million of the chips to Chinese-tied companies across those applications, per the report.
The approvals, which don't necessarily indicate completed sales, included 75,000 for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent and its subsidiaries, 43,000 for Baidu, and 4,000 for BYD, according to the report. Each of those companies has been identified by the Defense Department as having ties to the Chinese military.
The report shows the Commerce Department has a “long track record of transparency with Congress about licensing activity for the H200 and equivalent chips, including both approvals and rejections,” a spokesperson for the Bureau of Industry and Security said in a statement Friday.
The spokesperson said the Commerce Department's approach to H200 licensing is based on a rule in the Federal Register that was published in January. The rule imposes “significant additional national security-related requirements on license applicants in order to qualify for case-by-case consideration rather than a presumption of denial,” the spokesperson said.
An Nvidia spokesperson said in a statement Friday that the “limited shipments we made under the H200 program were legal and authorized” by the BIS. “The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes," the company spokesperson said.
Earlier this week, Nvidia said it was no longer shipping H200 chips to China. The spokesperson said Friday that shipments had stopped despite prior approvals.
AMD said it complies with U.S. export control laws and regulations and maintains “rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations” in a statement from a spokesperson Friday. “We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity,” the spokesperson said.
Chinese technology firms have been bracing for impacts on their ambitious AI development plans as scrutiny mounts on export controls in the U.S.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been under intense scrutiny himself in the wake of the turmoil following the Huang affair. Last week, Bessent said he was frustrated with the Commerce Department’s delay in placing restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to Megaspeed International, which is under investigation by the U.S. for potentially diverting restricted Nvidia AI chips to China. A former executive at the company who allegedly had an affair with Huang was reportedly suspected by U.S. intelligence agencies of being a spy for China.
In an unusually public rebuke of a fellow Cabinet member, Bessent said his department wanted to place export controls on Megaspeed, but Commerce was in charge of the matter.
Speaking to reporters on Friday, Trump said he has “not lost confidence” in Lutnick. Calling him a “different kind of guy," Trump said he “has a natural business instinct” and has “done a very good job.”
Huamani reported from Los Angeles. Associated Press writer Meg Kinnard contributed from Columbia, South Carolina.

articles.title_orig: Trump Flaunts Camaraderie With Xi and Putin but Has Little to Show for It
articles.title_zh: Trump Flaunts Camaraderie With Xi and Putin but Has Little to Show for It
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump ’s warm greeting for Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China Thursday sparked concern and ire from some European lawmakers.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk appeared to mock Trump’s labeling of Putin as “ my friend ” with a pointed social media message that read : “God, protect us from such friends.”
The post was shared just hours before Tusk headed to a meeting in Berlin of the “ Coalition of the Willing ,” an initiative intended to bolster support for Ukraine more than four years after its invasion by Russia. Tusk joined leaders from Germany, France, Britain, and Italy, along with NATO chief Mark Rutte and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Also in attendance were U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who briefed the group on Trump’s meetings with Putin in China. The session saw Europe secure a seat at the negotiating table for the next stage of U.S.-mediated talks between Russian and Ukrainian delegations.
Tusk, meanwhile, made another apparent dig at Trump during the meeting as he posted a picture of himself sharing a laugh with Zelensky and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham alongside the caption: "True friendship."
Further critique came from Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski, who reportedly told the media: “The optics of this cosying up to Putin—calling him a 'friend'—cause us some concern, because it raises the question: with whom is he truly friends?”
Trump hailed his "great relationship" with Putin ahead of their historic trilateral sit-down with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Addressing Ukraine at the top of the meeting, Trump said: "I think things are happening. I think that he [Putin] and—I hope—the other side would like to see an end to that war.” However, the China-U.S.-Russia “peace declaration” published by Chinese state media after the trilateral summit notably included no mention of Ukraine.
European leaders vowed to support Ukraine "for as long as it takes" at the close of the session in Berlin.
Emphasizing the need for Europe to be involved in talks moving forward, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told reporters: "Should peace negotiations take place, we will be involved. Negotiations can only succeed if Ukraine and Europe are part of the process together. A 'Yalta-style' format will not bring about peace.”
With negotiations between Russian and Ukrainian delegations over territory deadlocked, U.S. mediators have sought to instead steer discussions toward post-war security guarantees and reconstruction. In line with this, Kushner told reporters that the U.S. is open to giving Ukraine NATO-like security guarantees.
"I will say from America’s perspective, giving an Article 5-like security guarantee is a really, really big deal. And I think that that’s something that President Trump is open to, but obviously it has to be in America’s interest to do that," he said, before going on to claim that Russia is “comfortable” with the idea, also.
Kushner added that Trump had called into the meeting to join the discussions with European leaders.
TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
Zelensky celebrated the assured inclusion of Europe in future negotiations, which are set to look at the continent’s wider security arrangements.
"Europe will be represented by five countries plus the European Union and NATO, and America fully understands why strong and coordinated European participation in the negotiations is necessary," he said .
The wartime leader went on to express the need for progress to be made ahead of Ukraine being plunged into its fifth winter at-war.
"We must take the necessary steps to ensure that Russia engages in serious, substantive work instead of wasting time. This is very important to us because people are dying—our Ukrainians," he urged. "Pressure is needed. Europe is ready with new sanctions and new steps to support Ukraine and the Ukrainian people. It is important that the United States of America exert its influence on Russia."
Donald Tusk, Andy Burnham, Volodymyr Zelensky, Friedrich Merz, Emmanuel Macron, Giorgia Meloni, and Bart De Wever are seated at the "Coalition of the Willing" meeting in Berlin on Nov. 19, 2026. Kay Nietfeld—AP
While European leaders have banded together to place further sanctions on Russia, in a bid to ramp up economic pressure on the Kremlin to end the war, there has been growing concern over Trump’s approach to Putin.
Last month, Trump waived sanctions on Russia in order to progress the controversial diesel deal he made with Putin in an attempt to lower fuel prices, which have soared in the wake of his war with Iran.
Amid the deal, Trump announced an “energy cease-fire” between Russia and Ukraine on Oct. 11, calling on the two countries to stop targeting each other’s assets. Zelensky accused Moscow of breaking the apparent agreement and resumed strikes against Russian oil facilities, defying pressure from Washington. Trump called Ukraine's fresh wave of strikes a " disgrace " and said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with than Putin."
After meeting with Putin in Russia last week, Witkoff told reporters that he thought "progress" had been made, but Russia and Ukraine have traded strikes in the days since. The sit-down in Moscow came after two days of U.S.-led talks between Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi yielded no major breakthroughs.
Meanwhile, the European Union’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Monday that ministers had approved new listings to target Russian refineries, banks, e-commerce, and companies that support Russia’s shadow fleet, a network of vessels that help Moscow evade sanctions on energy exports. Kallas added that the 22nd sanctions package against Russia would be presented in-full within the next few days.
The united response and continued economic pressure from Europe stands in stark contrast to how the Trump Administration is currently dealing with Putin.
Further tensions between Europe and Washington have stemmed from the early days of the Iran war, after European leaders refused to actively get involved in the conflict—earning public rebuke from Trump. The global energy crisis that has since ensued, and the soaring fuel costs, has also soured relations. Other topics of contention include NATO spending and tariff rows .
The Democrats’ sweeping victories in the midterm elections earlier this month were viewed by some European leaders as a rebuke of Trump and his Administration’s policies. “American society voted against policies that only make people poorer. Against hate. Against sexism. Against climate denial and against elite privilege,” said Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who has previously clashed with Trump .

articles.title_orig: CrowdStrike in talks to acquire Zscaler, sources say
articles.title_zh: CrowdStrike in talks to acquire Zscaler, sources say
articles.content_orig:
Zscaler shares surged 18% in extended trading on Friday after Bloomberg reported that CrowdStrike is in talks to buy the cybersecurity vendor. Shares of CrowdStrike shares fell more than 8%.
The talks between the two companies are ongoing, Bloomberg reported, citing sources familiar in the matter. CrowdStrike declined to comment on the report. Zscaler didn't immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
CrowdStrike has been one of the big cybersecurity winners in the artificial intelligence boom, with its stock about doubling in value this year, lifting its market cap to $235 billion. Zscaler, meanwhile, is down 13% this year, pushing its market cap down to about $32 billion.
Along with CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks has seen its business boom as businesses race to upgrade their networks in the AI era. Palo Alto closed Friday at a nearly $282 billion market cap.
Should a deal take place, it would be among the largest in the history of the cybersecurity industry. Google acquired Wiz last year for $32 billion. In 2024, Cisco paid about $28 billion for Splunk. Earlier this year, Palo Alto closed its purchase of CyberArk for $25 billion .
CrowdStrike's deals to this point have been on the smaller side.The company announced plans earlier this month to acquire agentic observability platform Fiddler AI and AI trust platform Dreadnode.

articles.title_orig: Google Is Killing the Nest App. Here’s What Comes Next
articles.title_zh: Google Is Killing the Nest App. Here’s What Comes Next
articles.content_orig:
Google is making some big changes to its smart home offerings, including killing the Nest app.﻿
Google is making some big changes to its smart home offerings, including killing the Nest app.﻿
Google is announcing some significant changes to its smart home software. Starting next year, the company will shut down the Nest app in favor of the Google Home app and retire Google Assistant on its smart home devices.
The Nest app shutdown takes place on January 25th, 2027, meaning you’ll have to manage your Nest products, including Nest thermostats, cameras, and Nest Protect alarms, from the Google Home app instead. If you get the Google Home app set up, Google will move over your Nest devices, including cameras and video history, to the Home app on that January 25th date. The company will also automatically transfer Nest Aware (1st Gen) subscriptions to Google Home Premium. Google says it will begin deleting Nest account data on March 25th, 2027.
The changes for Google Assistant will take place later: On August 2nd, 2027, the Gemini for Home voice assistant will replace Google Assistant on smart speakers and smart displays, the company says. Google argues that Gemini for Home allows users to ask more complex questions and speak naturally instead of needing to use dedicated commands or specific language.
Gemini for Home was announced last year , so it’s not exactly a shock that Google is going to move on from Google Assistant in the smart home (especially when the company also killed Google Assistant on phones earlier this year ). The company says it plans to share more updates about the changes ahead of the August 2027 transition.

The Cboe Volatility Index, better known as the VIX, touched 40 late in the session as stocks extended their slide late in the day, the highest level for the gauge of expected S&P 500 price swings since the tariff turmoil. But while traders are having to pay up for option contracts to protect against bigger swings, there's little sign of panic in the broader market.
The rise in the VIX was more of a mechanical response to the 3.6% fall in the S&P 500 than because of a desperate rush to buy more protection, according to Mandy Xu, head of derivatives market intelligence at the Cboe Global Markets Inc., which created the gauge. "There's a lot more uncertainty in the near term, but not necessarily a lot more fear."
She said that more than four-fifths of the move was due to the drop in the S&P 500 and the knock-on effect that had on the pricing of longer-dated options, rather than because of demand for downside protection.
While the VIX moving into the 30s is a signal of market stress, such events typically happen several times a year, and rarely for more than a few days at a time.
Still, some investors are betting that volatility will persist.
"Conditions may be ripe for a big right tail move in the VIX," Matthew Thompson, managing partner at Thompson Capital Management, said in a call around noon New York time on Friday. The VIX added nine more points on Friday afternoon to briefly touch 40.
The firm is now long index volatility using VIX futures contracts.

articles.title_orig: AI tech rout prompts US investors to rush into value stocks
articles.title_zh: AI tech rout prompts US investors to rush into value stocks
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic’s stock market debut turned the vast majority of the young startup’s staff into overnight millionaires — some many times over.
The company’s headcount stood at 5,300 as of September this year, according to regulatory filings. After Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share, about 600 employees entered the rarefied “centi-millionaire” club, with equity holdings valued north of $100 million, according to data from Hill.com , which tracks private-company shares.
As many as 2,800 staffers, known internally as “Ants,” have holdings valued above $10 million. And about 5,100 — 96% of the staff — are sitting on equity north of $1 million.
“What’s most surprising here is how quickly this this happened,” Andrew Benson, Hill’s founder and CEO, told CNN on Thursday, noting Anthropic has seen very little attrition. “It’s been pretty clear for some time that Anthropic is a rocket ship, and so it definitely discouraged people from leaving because they knew what the opportunity cost of that would be.”
Anthropic valued at $1.76 trillion after first day of trading
It’s not unusual for Silicon Valley startups, which are typically light on cash, to pay their staff with a combination of salary and stock. The promise of a future acquisition or initial public offering tends to keep workers motivated to work hard and stick it out until payday.
But few startups have grown as big or as quickly as Anthropic. The company, founded in 2021, had fewer than 1,000 employees at the end of 2024.
As with most tech startups, Benson noted, “being early is more important, in terms of a financial outcome, than being senior … You could be very low on the totem pole, and if you joined in 2023 or 2024, you’re likely to have a significantly better outcome than a senior person who joined earlier this year.”
SpaceX, by contrast, spent more than two decades as a private company before its blockbuster IPO in June. That debut minted around 4,400 millionaires, out of a staff of 22,000.
Anthropic’s IPO is also unique for allowing non-founder insiders to cash out on Day One of trading. In most IPOs, staff are subject to a “lockup” period — typically three to six months — during which they can’t sell their shares. But Anthropic’s listing included a complex, staggered lockup schedule that allowed non-founder insiders to cash out up to 10% of their shares as soon as the stock began trading. (It’s not known how many insiders may have taken advantage of the opportunity Thursday.)
And unlike SpaceX, which has employees spread across Texas, California and Florida, Anthropic is uniquely concentrated in San Francisco, a city whose entire economy has been reshaped by sudden surges of tech wealth.
A rash of newly minted millionaires could soon amplify pressure on San Francisco’s housing market, where home prices are already rising at their fastest pace in years.
The typical home there sold for $1.7 million in October, up nearly 19% from a year earlier, according to Redfin. By contrast, the national median home price was roughly flat over the same period, at $416,700, according to the National Association of Realtors.
CNN’s Samantha Delouya contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: US tech stocks plunge into bear market in worst week since Covid-19 crisis
articles.title_zh: US tech stocks plunge into bear market in worst week since Covid-19 crisis
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
NEW YORK, Nov 20 (Reuters) - Tumbling technology-related shares led a global stock sell off on Friday, with US traders searching for safe havens as the US 10-year yield dropped by the most in a month.
Traders ‌sold stocks in most markets with Japan and Korea down more than 5% overnight. Taiwanese shares were down 17% for the week, ‌their biggest weekly decline since 1990, while on Wall Street chip-maker shares fell 10.7% Friday and 17.1% for the week.
Anthropic, which debuted this week, fell as much as ​14.5% on its first full day of trading, just above its $83 IPO pricing, and ended down 9.1% at $88.30.
Consumer staples was the sole S&P 500 sector to end in the black on Friday.
"Markets are entering a more defensive phase," said Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at Capital.com.
"Strong AI demand and successful individual listings are no longer sufficient to sustain broader risk appetite when investors are questioning valuations, borrowing costs and the ‌outlook for corporate profitability."
The Dow Jones Industrial ⁠Average fell 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33; the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points, or 3.70%, to 6,910.39, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 1,261.47 points, or 5.28%, to 22,617.73.
MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe ⁠fell 34.89 points, or 3.30%, to 1,021.91. Its weekly decline of 8.1% was the largest since early 2020.
The pan-European STOXX 600 index fell 2%, emerging market stocks fell 3.10% and MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan closed lower by 3.27%. Japan's Nikkei fell 5.06%.
The VIX index, linked to ​the cost ​of insurance against a drop in the S&P 500, closed at its highest ​since April 2025.
As investors sought safe-haven assets, government bonds ‌rallied.
The yield on benchmark US 10-year notes fell 10.43 basis points to 4.948%, the largest daily drop since October 22. The 30-year bond yield fell 6.81 basis points to 5.3329%. The 2-year note yield, which typically moves in step with interest rate expectations for the Federal Reserve, fell 13.21 basis points to 4.647% even as a rate hike is priced in for next month's policy meeting.
DOLLAR FLAT, OIL RISES LATE
The dollar index was little changed after touching a 19-month high on Thursday. The dollar's recent rally has been fueled by bets on ‌tighter monetary policy due to hotter-than-expected US inflation data.
"I think the momentum ​has stalled for the dollar ... but I think it's a little bit early to ​pick a top for the dollar," said Marc Chandler, ​chief market strategist at Bannockburn Capital Markets.
The dollar index fell 0.05% to 103.90, with the euro down ‌0.05% at $1.0961. Against the Japanese yen, the dollar weakened 0.67% ​to 158.6.
In commodities, crude prices ​rose late on Friday on worries about possible attacks in the US-Israeli war with Iran, and as traders bought crude ahead of next week's Thanksgiving holiday.
US crude rose 1.49% to $83.67 a barrel and Brent rose to $92.61 per barrel, up 0.68% on the ​day.
Gold prices fell to a 14-month low ‌after the largest weekly drop in 8 months.
Spot gold fell 2.81% to $3,520.09 an ounce and spot silver fell 4.22% ​to $40.95 an ounce. Copper declined 2.9% to $12,162.50 a ton.
(Reporting by Rodrigo Campos, Harry Robertson, Anna Hirtenstein, Saqib Iqbal Ahmed; ​editing by Xevi Fontdegloria, Mark Potter, Nick Zieminski and Jonathan Spicer )

articles.title_orig: Anthropic stock drops 8% after rip-roaring IPO
articles.title_zh: Anthropic stock drops 8% after rip-roaring IPO
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Call it the Anthropic ( ANT ) IPO hangover.
Shares of the model builder dropped nearly 8.5% on Friday as investors booked profits after a frenetic first day of trading. Not helping sentiment: The broader market plunged on Anthropic's well-received IPO day and remains under pressure today.
Follow live updates amid Friday's worst sell-off since 2025.
Anthropic made a monster debut on Wall Street Thursday, with shares opening at $111.50 a little before noon ET, a 34% premium to the $83 IPO price.
But the AI company's stock couldn't hold on to its early gains.
The stock closed at $97.17, up 17% on the day. That closing price gave Anthropic a market capitalization of about $1.28 trillion, or roughly $1.75 trillion on a fully diluted basis. Not bad for a company founded only five years ago, in a historic IPO that raised $81.3 billion.
On Friday, the stock closed just below $89 per share with a market cap of $1.17 trillion.
"At a time in which investors are very nervous on the overall tech trade and the Nvidia black cloud moment casts a shadow over the tech sector, Anthropic's debut is a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning," Yorkville Ives partner Dan Ives said.

articles.title_orig: Trump asks Nvidia to give Jensen Huang a ‘second chance’
articles.title_zh: Trump asks Nvidia to give Jensen Huang a ‘second chance’
articles.content_orig:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang will testify publicly when he appears before the Senate banking panel, a spokesperson for Committee Chair Tim Scott said Friday.
The South Carolina Republican confirmed earlier this week that Huang had agreed to appear, but the details of that appearance remained unclear. Huang, who resigned from the company he co-founded earlier this month over a series of extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, also reached an agreement with three House committees to appear for a closed-door, transcribed interview on Dec. 1.
The date of Huang's public testimony in the Senate has not yet been announced, though Scott initially requested he appear on Dec. 3.
His office did not respond when asked when Huang would appear. Scott told CNBC on Wednesday he hopes to hear testimony from Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick "before Christmas." The new Congress, when Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., is expected to take over as Senate banking chair, convenes Jan. 3.

articles.title_orig: Markets plunge: Nasdaq erases 2026 gains, S&P and Dow enter corrections
articles.title_zh: Markets plunge: Nasdaq erases 2026 gains, S&P and Dow enter corrections
articles.content_orig:
The surging stock market of 2026 capsized Friday, wiping out gains for the year in the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite while the broad S&P 500 and the Dow entered correction territory, meaning they have declined 10% from recent peaks.
The dramatic sell-off is raising fresh fears about the viability of the AI investment wave that had powered stocks and economic growth for the first half of the year.
Friday’s declines were led by Anthropic, whose blockbuster IPO just 24 hours earlier now feels like a blip after the stock lost 9%, wiping out hundreds of billions in paper wealth and putting shares just a few dollars above the IPO price.
Nvidia also dragged markets lower, tumbling about 14% following a Reuters report that regulators are looking into accounting irregularities at the chip giant.
With Friday’s losses of 3.7%, the S&P 500’s seven-day losing streak is its worst since the Covid pandemic; the index is now up less than 1% on the year.
The Nasdaq finished the day down 5.3%, and the Dow dropped 1.9%.
The losses also sully one of the most visible bright points of President Donald Trump’s second term. Amid sticky inflation and frozen housing and jobs markets, U.S. equities were the one part of the economy that appeared resilient. The AI investment boom created seemingly insatiable demand for stocks among investors, minting multiple new trillion-dollar companies in the process.
While Friday’s declines were stark, they were not sudden, capping instead a weekslong slide that began in early October as the combination of elevated oil prices , rising interest rates , mounting corporate debt loads , stubborn inflation , supply chain issues and a flagging consumer put increasing pressure on stock prices.
The sell-off picked up steam earlier this month in the wake of Democrats’ midterm victories, which raised fears of a slowdown in the tech sector’s data center buildout. Losses accelerated again last week as the scandal erupted involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and advanced chips potentially being diverted to China.
“The stock market is going through an AI repricing, reflecting an environment of slowing data center buildouts, reduced funding sources for AI-related projects and a slower trajectory of technology-related earnings growth,” wrote Richard Saperstein, chief investment officer at Treasury Partners, in a client note. “This has been exacerbated by the Nvidia crisis and the Democratic midterm win, which were a one-two punch for the AI story.”
Alongside the stock sell-off, investors have increased purchases of U.S. Treasury bonds — a sign that investors are seeking more reliable returns amid signs of weakening growth from higher interest rates and a stalling economy in China.
“The pressure is becoming increasingly widespread, and that’s been felt across other asset classes too,” Deutsche Bank managing director Jim Reid wrote in a note to clients Friday.
For U.S. households relying on 401(k)s and pension funds for retirement, the downturn is especially unwelcome at a time when inflation continues to prove nettlesome.
Kevin Gordon, head of macroeconomic strategy and research at Charles Schwab, told NBC News that markets are feeling particular pressure from an increasingly “hawkish” Federal Reserve that is signaling aggressive rate hikes in the face of unrelenting inflation.
“They’re signaling that they want to be aggressive in raising rates,” Gordon said. Combined with a weeks-long downturn among AI and tech stocks, “we have dual forces hitting the market.”
A prolonged downturn could begin to cut more deeply into economic growth, he said.
“If you have enough of a protracted downturn, which we really haven’t had since 2007-2009 in terms of length and duration, that’s when you’d really start to worry,” he said.
Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.

articles.title_orig: Trump floats an unexpected name to be his successor as powerhouses Rubio and Vance stand by
articles.title_zh: Trump floats an unexpected name to be his successor as powerhouses Rubio and Vance stand by
articles.content_orig:
Chief of staff Stephen Miller praises President Trump's record on deregulation and the economy, and Trump jokingly asks if he wants to run for president.
During a lighthearted Friday afternoon moment with the media inside the White House press briefing room, President Donald Trump floated a new name to succeed him as president, while two expected 2028 hopefuls stood by.
The president asked the media if they'd like to continue with the press conference — where Trump provided updates on his trip to China where he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. This prompted laughs from Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who flanked him on either side during the briefing.
Then, he asked newly-minted Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, whom he called the "most powerful man in the world," to speak with members of the press.
MAGA VOTERS REVEAL WHO THEY WANT TO SEE LEAD GOP IN 2028
President Donald Trump speaks as Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio look on during a news briefing in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House on Nov. 20, 2026, in Washington, D.C. Trump addressed the media after returning from a visit to China where he held trilateral talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
Miller took the podium and launched into a more than two-minute speech listing Trump's accomplishments from the first two years of his second term in office.
"I just wanted to say that what President Trump has achieved over the last two years is more than any president has achieved by far in American history. We can stand up here for four hours and go through achievement by achievement by achievement," Miller said.
He then rattled some of them off, including:
White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller speaks during a press briefing at the White House, Thursday, May 1, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)
"Under his leadership, the next two years are going to be the greatest two years in American history," Miller said. "And I'm so proud to be his chief of staff to oversee on his behalf the staff in this building to keep delivering wins for this extraordinary American leader."
Trump was clearly impressed with Miller, who stepped in to replace Susie Wiles earlier this month following sweeping midterm losses for Republicans.
"We have breaking news! Breaking news!" Trump said. "He was better than these two guys," he added, turning towards Vance and Rubio, who both also spoke at the press conference.
"Do you want to run for president?" Trump asked Miller as he was leaving the podium, prompting laughter from the group.
STEPHEN MILLER'S INTERNAL MEMO UNLEASHES TRUMP AGENCIES AFTER 'ABSOLUTE CONTROL' UNDER WILES' REIGN
Vice President JD Vance, President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio attend a news conference in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Friday, Nov. 20, 2026. Trump vowed to tax American companies that build data centers in other countries, though he did not detail how such a threat would be carried out or what legal authority the government might have to impose one. (Yuri Gripas/CNP/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
No major names from either party have yet to announce their intentions to run for president in 2028 . But with the midterms finished, rumors have swirled about who will toss their hats in the ring.
Vance and Rubio are widely viewed as the two most viable options for Republicans.

Miller's name has not been previously floated as a contender for launching a White House bid.
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

articles.title_zh: Wired headphones are making a major comeback — here’s why, plus 5 of the best pairs you can buy
articles.content_orig:
NBC Selected independently determines what we cover and recommend. When you click on or buy through our links, we earn a commission. Learn more .
For most of the last decade, corded headphones have been nearly nonexistent. Phone makers dropped the headphone jack, AirPods became the go-to, and a tangle of wire hanging from your ears started to look dated. Now the cord is making a comeback.
After five straight years of falling sales, wired headphone purchases climbed sharply in the second half of 2025, according to the market research firm Circana , and revenue from the category was up about 20% in the first six weeks of 2026. The trend is visible, too: Wired earbuds have been showing up on TikTok and Instagram feeds and Bose released its first wired earbuds in 11 years this fall — and the first batch sold out quickly.
If you are interested in kicking it old school with a pair of wired headphones, keep reading, I’ve rounded up top-rated styles worth your consideration.
Every pick on this list connects with a cable. I included a mix of over-ear headphones, on-ear headphones and earbuds. I’ve included options that NBC Selected editors love, as well as highly rated options that have a minimum four-star average rating from one hundred or more shoppers.
If the wired comeback has an icon, it’s Apple’s white EarPods. More than 10,000 pairs sold on Amazon in the past month alone. I bought a pair recently after NBC Selected senior editor Nikki Brown mentioned she had switched back to using them because they’re affordable and less easy to lose. I’ve loved using them to make calls, listen to podcasts and more. When not in use, I love that I can wrap them around my phone.
The newest version uses a USB-C plug, so it works with the iPhone 15 and newer, plus most Android phones and laptops, without a dongle. Apple still sells lightning and 3.5mm versions, too. The sound is clear and pleasant and the open design lets in surrounding noise, which some people like for walking or biking around a busy city.
Bose launched these in October 2026, its first wired earbuds in 11 years. They connect over USB-C and an in-line remote handles volume, calls and noise-canceling modes. The only other earbuds on this list (besides EarPods), these come with three eartip sizes and two stability bands to help you find a secure fit. They’re also IPX4 sweat-resistant.
The ATH-M50x is a go-to studio headphone and it’s just as popular with everyday listeners because it delivers balanced sound. The foam ear cups keep your music in and outside noise out, which makes it practical for an office or a commute. And the detachable cables are a big selling point. Cords are the most common failure point on wired headphones, and with the M50x you can swap in a new one at no extra cost: . It  comes with three, including a coiled cable (for desks and studios) and a straight one (for on the go).
Koss introduced the Porta Pro in 1984, and it has barely changed since. The chunky foam earpads and metal headband look like they came straight from a Walkman ad, which has made them a favorite among people leaning into the retro side of the wired revival. Reviewers like bass-forward sound and value, and Koss backs them with a lifetime warranty. Just know that because the earcups are open, the people next to you will hear some of what you’re listening to.
If you’re a sound snob, these headphones from Sennheiser are worth considering. Reviewers call the crisp, clear sound of these “incredible,” and say they have “impressive clarity.” The over-ear design creates a spacious, natural sound, almost like listening to speakers in the room. They are also lightweight and velour ear pads keep you comfortable for hours-long wear.

articles.title_orig: How Carney’s Shift Toward China Could Become Leverage in Stalled U.S. Trade Talks
articles.title_zh: How Carney’s Shift Toward China Could Become Leverage in Stalled U.S. Trade Talks
articles.content_orig:
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney shakes hands with China's President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit on Nov. 19, 2026.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is placing particular focus on renewing relations with China as he aims to deepen international trade ties and diversify from U.S. reliance amid a three-month-long trade war with the U.S.
When asked what cards Canada holds in its ongoing talks with Washington, Carney, who recently announced a new partnership with the E.U. , pointed to the country's budding relationships elsewhere.
“Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” he said Wednesday during a remote interview with the New York Times from Shenzhen, China, where he was among the world leaders attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit . "If the U.S. doesn't want to do the deal, we're busy.” His remarks came in the wake of President Donald Trump's claim that the U.S. holds “all the cards” after trade talks collapsed in August, leading to both sides enforcing heavy retaliatory tariffs .
Carney and Trump had a meeting on the sidelines of APEC, but aside from a commitment to “continue” negotiations and stay in close contact, no progress was made. However, Carney painted his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in a much more positive light. Ahead of the summit, Carney and Xi announced a Canada-China trade pact , which provided additional tariff relief on Canadian food and agricultural exports into China, and in return saw Canada agree to extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years.
Carney, who is promoting a “Canada Strong” platform as he aims to build economic resilience at home, touted the expansion of the trade arrangement with China as something that will deliver “greater certainty and prosperity for all Canadians.” He also praised the negotiation process with China, saying: “They’re very professional. They move forward in a very linear fashion.”
In an eight-day tour that took him from a European summit in Ireland to the Philippines, Cambodia, and finally China for the APEC gathering, Carney forged ahead with his plan to diversify Canada's economy away from its dependence on the U.S., which by far remains the country's largest trading partner .
Experts say Canada's progress in deepening its economic relationships with China could challenge Trump's insistence that Washington holds the upper hand in trade negotiations.
“Part of the Trump Administration’s [belief] is that everybody needs the U.S. more than anything else, and therefore the U.S. has maximum leverage,” says Jennifer Hillman, co-director of the Institute of International Economic Law at Georgetown University. “What this is clearly saying is that Canada can afford to be less willing to give the U.S. whatever it asks for [in negotiations], because they have other options.”
China has the world's second-largest economy , behind only the U.S., giving it the potential to become a much larger market for Canadian goods than some of the other countries Carney has sought to deepen relations with.
“China represents a very big market and the potential of a really big trading partner,” says Lori Turnbull, a professor in the Faculty of Management at Dalhousie University, noting it could be a leverage point in U.S. negotiations. “Doing a deal with a country like China is something that [the U.S.] will care about because of the size of China's economy and its competitive relationship with the U.S.”
Carney's latest push to strengthen trade ties with Beijing forms part of a months-long effort to renew Canada-China relations. In January, he met with Xi to forge what he called a “ new strategic partnership ,” agreeing to allow in up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a tariff of 6.1%, rather than the previous 100% levy. China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
The move drew criticism from Trump, who said that “China will eat Canada alive, completely devour it, including the destruction of their businesses, social fabric, and general way of life.”
While Canada's closer relationship with China could strengthen its hand in negotiations, experts also warn that it could backfire.
Turnbull points to the latest agreement to extend tariff exemptions on Chinese steel and aluminum as a potential source of tension with Washington. “Things like reducing tariffs on select steel and aluminum products coming from China is something that might make the U.S. and not just Donald Trump, but also [U.S. Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer angry,” she suggests.
Steel, aluminum, and auto tariffs were among the major points of contention when U.S.-Canada trade negotiations broke down in August, with both sides accusing each other of walking back commitments.
Carney, however, has played down concerns that Canada's growing trade relationship with China is a major issue for Trump.
“In my conversation with the President, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”
Meanwhile, some Canadian officials have voiced concerns on expanding trade with China.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford warned Carney on Monday against opening the door for more Chinese-made EV vehicles in Canada, arguing the “government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars.”
Michael Chong, a lawmaker from Canada’s Conservative Party, during a press conference on Wednesday supported maintaining a dialogue with Beijing, but described Carney’s budding strategic partnership with China as a “risky gambit,” citing potential “national security” concerns.
In 2025, Ottawa identified China as one of the main perpetrators of foreign interference and espionage against Canada alongside other countries such as Russia and Iran. The Canadian government’s own analysis of Canada-China relations also points out that there are "associated risks” in broader trade cooperation in key areas, such as “prevalent and persistent intellectual property theft, and the risk of diversion of sensitive goods and technologies intended for civilian use for military purposes and applications.”
Carney said ahead of his Asia trip that he would raise concerns about foreign interference in his meeting with Xi. "The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly,” he told reporters in Montreal on Nov. 10. Carney added that he would stress the importance Canada places on "the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries.”
In a press briefing during the APEC summit, Carney emphasized that Canada's trade with China is largely focused on commodities, rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.
“We are exporting canola, we are exporting pork. We are exporting halibut,” Carney said , also citing liquefied natural gas and oil. “These are important industries. These are not cutting-edge semi-conductors.”
Experts point out that Canada could pursue deeper cooperation with other international partners in sectors where a closer relationship with China would be more difficult, including defense and advanced technology.
“[Canada] is not going to partner with China on defense, security, AI, and digital technology, things like that would be very difficult. [Carney] would have an impossible time trying to convince Canadians that's what we should be doing,” says Turnbull. “For those things, [Canada] would be putting [its] arms around the European Union.”
In September, the European Union unveiled its vision for Canada to become an “associate member” of the bloc. During an E.U.-Canada summit in Montreal in October, the two sides underscored their commitment to this plan, paving the way for deeper cooperation in areas including A

articles.title_orig: China takes centre stage at trilateral with US, Russia
articles.title_zh: China takes centre stage at trilateral with US, Russia
articles.content_orig:
Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’
China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.
The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.
Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.
The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.
“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.
Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.
First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”
The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.
Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”
Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce .
Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.
European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.
The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.
Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.
Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.
Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.
